person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: serum concentrations of twelve polyfluoroalkyl chemicals in a representative sample of the U.S. population aged 12 and over
span.quote: Four analytes were detected in > 98% of the samples (PFOS, 99.9%; PFOA, 99.7%; PFHxS, 98.3%; PFNA, 98.8%).

span.label: whether U.S. population exposure to PFCs changed after the 2002 discontinuation of PFOS production
span.quote: Biomonitoring data for these PFCs in the general population are needed to assess current exposures and to determine whether technologic changes affect human exposures to these compounds.

span.label: the first nationally representative PFC serum estimates after the manufacturing change, with a method-equivalence check spanning the two survey waves
span.quote: We analyzed the NHANES 1999–2000 and 2003–2004 samples by using two different methods; however, these approaches provided equivalent results [Table 1; Figures S1 and S2 in the Supplemental Material (online at http://www.ehponline.org/docs/2007/10598/suppl.pdf)], indicating that the differences cannot be attributed to changes in the analytical methodology.

span.label: existence
span.quote: Four analytes were detected in > 98% of the samples (PFOS, 99.9%; PFOA, 99.7%; PFHxS, 98.3%; PFNA, 98.8%).

span.label: population-wide, measurable exposure to persistent fluorinated chemicals, declining for three compounds and rising for one
span.quote: The apparent reductions in concentrations of PFOS, PFOA, and PFHxS most likely are related to discontinuation in 2002 of industrial production by electrochemical fluorination of PFOS and related perfluorooctanesulfonyl fluoride compounds.

span.label: isotope-dilution HPLC-tandem mass spectrometry on 2,094 NHANES serum samples, with survey-weighted regression
span.term: isotope-dilution HPLC-tandem mass spectrometry on 2,094 NHANES serum samples, with survey-weighted regression
span.quote: To compensate for the lack of isotope-labeled internal standards for the other analytes and to partially account for matrix effects, the calibration standards were spiked into calf serum.

span.label: electrochemical fluorination of PFOS and related compounds stopped in 2002, and three of the four common PFCs show lower geometric means four years later
span.quote: The apparent reductions in concentrations of PFOS, PFOA, and PFHxS most likely are related to discontinuation in 2002 of industrial production by electrochemical fluorination of PFOS and related perfluorooctanesulfonyl fluoride compounds.

span.label: PFHxS declines least because it clears slowest - 7.3 years against 4.8 for PFOS and 3.5 for PFOA - so the same phase-out shows up later in it
span.quote: These findings may be related to the lower concentrations of PFHxS than of PFOS or PFOA and to differences in the estimated geometric mean serum elimination half-life (PFHxS, 7.3 years; PFOA, 3.5 years; and PFOS, 4.8 years).

span.label: PFOS and PFOA correlate more strongly with each other than either does with PFHxS, which the authors read as a shared source that PFHxS does not have
span.quote: Furthermore, the correlation between the serum concentrations of PFOS and PFOA was higher than correlations of PFHxS and either PFOA or PFOS, suggesting potential common exposure path-way(s) for PFOA and PFOS, but probably not for PFHxS

span.label: PFHxS is higher in adolescents than adults, and the proposed reason is contact with carpets treated with it - a route specific to one compound
span.quote: The higher concentrations of PFHxS in children and adolescents could be related to their increased contact with carpeted floors containing PFHxS, which is used for specific postmarket carpet-treatment applications.

span.label: PFNA doubled, and the authors say human exposure data for it are too limited to interpret the rise confidently
span.quote: Interestingly, our data suggest that PFNA geometric mean concentrations in 2003–2004 approximately doubled over those of 1999–2000. However, because human exposure data for PFNA are more limited than they are for PFOS, PFOA, and even PFHxS, these results must be interpreted with caution.

span.label: for the two rarest analytes no 95th percentile could be calculated at all
span.quote: For the two analytes detected in < 1% of the samples (PFDoA, < 0.1%; PFBuS, 0.4%), we could not calculate the 95th percentile of concentrations.

span.label: no definite association between PFOS or PFOA exposure and adverse health effects has been established in humans
span.quote: No definite association has been established between exposure to PFOS and PFOA and adverse health effects in several occupational studies and in one population exposed to PFOA through contaminated drinking water.

span.label: the animal effects that motivate concern occur at serum concentrations orders of magnitude above those measured here
span.quote: In animals, exposure to PFOS and PFOA is associated with adverse health effects albeit at serum concentrations orders of magnitude higher than the concentrations observed in the general population.

span.label: the persistent-organic-pollutant framework, carried from chlorinated chemicals to fluorinated ones, including the expectation that concentrations rise with age - which fails here
span.quote: For PFOS, PFOA, and PFNA, however—unlike lipophilic POPs whose serum concentrations increase with age —concentrations were quite similar among the four age groups (Tables 2–5), a finding that agrees with previous data.

span.label: 124 split samples run through BOTH analytical methods, to test whether the method change between survey waves produced the trend
span.note: eliminates: a fall in serum concentrations that is a change of analytical method between survey waves - the split samples make the two methods comparable on the same serum · outcome: held
span.quote: To estimate whether method differences could account for the differences in concentrations, we analyzed QC samples from low and high concentration pools and 124 split samples using both methods. The two methods showed good agreement from the results of the split sample analysis [presented for PFOA in Figures S1 and S2 in Supplemental Material (online at http://www.ehponline.org/docs/2007/10598/suppl.pdf)]. Results were similar for all other analytes (data not shown).

span.label: the explicit question of whether the decline is an artefact of changed methodology
span.note: eliminates: the same artefact, asked as a question of the result rather than of the instrument · outcome: held
span.quote: We analyzed the NHANES 1999–2000 and 2003–2004 samples by using two different methods; however, these approaches provided equivalent results [Table 1; Figures S1 and S2 in the Supplemental Material (online at http://www.ehponline.org/docs/2007/10598/suppl.pdf)], indicating that the differences cannot be attributed to changes in the analytical methodology.

span.label: calibration standards spiked into calf serum to account for matrix effects and the absence of labelled internal standards for most analytes
span.note: eliminates: a systematic bias from the serum matrix, or from the absence of an isotope-labelled internal standard for most analytes, being read as a concentration difference · outcome: held
span.quote: To compensate for the lack of isotope-labeled internal standards for the other analytes and to partially account for matrix effects, the calibration standards were spiked into calf serum.

span.label: low- and high-concentration quality-control pools run alongside reagent blank, serum blank and the samples
span.note: eliminates: analytical drift across a run being reported as variation between people · outcome: held
span.quote: Low-concentration (~ 3 μg/L to ~ 9 μg/L) and high-concentration (~ 10 μg/L to ~ 30 μg/L) quality-control (QC) materials, prepared from a base calf serum pool, were analyzed with reagent blank, serum blank, and NHANES samples.

span.label: agreement of the declines with independent series - Red Cross blood donors and Arctic ringed seals
span.note: eliminates: a decline confined to this survey's sampling frame - the seals and the blood donors share no methodology and no population with NHANES · outcome: held
span.quote: The decrease in serum concentrations of PFOS and PFOA during this time interval agreed with the reported reductions in PFOS and PFOA concentrations for a group of Red Cross blood donors in the United States and in PFOS (temporal trends for PFOA were not examined) in Arctic ringed seals in the same time.

span.label: confounding, tested by re-adding each excluded variable and watching the beta coefficients
span.note: eliminates: a coefficient that survives only under the authors' final choice of covariates · outcome: held
span.quote: We evaluated for potential confounding by adding each of the excluded variables back into the final model one by one and examining changes in the β coefficients of the statistically significant main effect. If addition of one of these excluded variables caused a change in a β coefficient by ≥ 10%, the variable was re-added to the model.

span.label: the split-sample comparison for analytes other than PFOA
span.note: eliminates: that the change in concentrations between survey rounds is a change in analytical method - answered for PFOA and left unshown for the other analytes · outcome: partial
span.quote: To estimate whether method differences could account for the differences in concentrations, we analyzed QC samples from low and high concentration pools and 124 split samples using both methods. The two methods showed good agreement from the results of the split sample analysis [presented for PFOA in Figures S1 and S2 in Supplemental Material (online at http://www.ehponline.org/docs/2007/10598/suppl.pdf)]. Results were similar for all other analytes (data not shown).

span.label: emission-reduction efforts for PFNA, the one compound that rose
span.note: eliminates: an emissions explanation for the one compound that ROSE - the reduction efforts that would provide it were looked for and not found, which the paper says · outcome: absent-declared-unreported
span.quote: Information about efforts to reduce manufacturing emissions for PFNA, estimated at about 10% of the amount produced, was not found. As a comparison, global manufacturing emissions of PFOA were about 15 tonnes in 2004, down from about 45 tonnes in 1999.

span.label: limits of detection
span.quote: The limits of detection (LODs) ranged from 0.1 to 1.0 μg/L; the accuracy ranged from 84 to 135% at three concentrations; and the precision ranged from around 10 to 26% at two different levels (Table 1).

span.label: geometric mean
span.quote: Interestingly, our data suggest that PFNA geometric mean concentrations in 2003–2004 approximately doubled over those of 1999–2000. However, because human exposure data for PFNA are more limited than they are for PFOS, PFOA, and even PFHxS, these results must be interpreted with caution.

span.label: Biomonitoring
span.quote: Biomonitoring data for these PFCs in the general population are needed to assess current exposures and to determine whether technologic changes affect human exposures to these compounds.

span.label: serum cotinine
span.quote: Participants were categorized as smokers if their serum cotinine concentrations were > 10 μg/L.

span.label: split samples
span.quote: To estimate whether method differences could account for the differences in concentrations, we analyzed QC samples from low and high concentration pools and 124 split samples using both methods. The two methods showed good agreement from the results of the split sample analysis [presented for PFOA in Figures S1 and S2 in Supplemental Material (online at http://www.ehponline.org/docs/2007/10598/suppl.pdf)]. Results were similar for all other analytes (data not shown).

span.label: PFBuS
span.quote: The lower frequency of detection of PFBuS than PFOS, PFOA, and PFHxS suggests that human exposures to PFBuS are indeed lower, and/or that pharmacokinetic factors, which might include increased urinary elimination, are different.

span.label: lipophilic POPs
span.quote: For PFOS, PFOA, and PFNA, however—unlike lipophilic POPs whose serum concentrations increase with age —concentrations were quite similar among the four age groups (Tables 2–5), a finding that agrees with previous data.

span.label: half-life
span.quote: These findings may be related to the lower concentrations of PFHxS than of PFOS or PFOA and to differences in the estimated geometric mean serum elimination half-life (PFHxS, 7.3 years; PFOA, 3.5 years; and PFOS, 4.8 years).

span.label: a NON-DETECT is entered as LOD divided by the square root of 2 - imputed, not measured
span.quote: For concentrations below the LOD, as recommended for the analysis of NHANES data, we used a value equal to the LOD divided by the square root of 2.

span.label: a mean is REPORTABLE only where the analyte was detected in at least 60% of samples
span.quote: Parametric statistics were computed only for analytes for which the frequency of detection was ≥ 60%.

span.label: a SMOKER is anyone with serum cotinine above 10 ug/L - a biomarker threshold, not self-report
span.quote: Participants were categorized as smokers if their serum cotinine concentrations were > 10 μg/L.

span.label: RACE/ETHNICITY is three self-reported categories, and everyone else is counted in the total but excluded from every subgroup comparison
span.quote: Race/ethnicity was defined on the basis of self-reported data as non-Hispanic black, non-Hispanic white, and Mexican American. Persons not defined by these groups were included only in the total population estimate.

span.label: a CONFOUNDER is a variable whose re-addition moves a beta coefficient by 10% or more
span.quote: We evaluated for potential confounding by adding each of the excluded variables back into the final model one by one and examining changes in the β coefficients of the statistically significant main effect. If addition of one of these excluded variables caused a change in a β coefficient by ≥ 10%, the variable was re-added to the model.

span.label: a RETAINED model term is one surviving backward elimination at p < 0.05
span.quote: To reach the final reduced model, we used backward elimination with a threshold of p < 0.05 for retaining the variable in the model, using Satterwaite adjusted F statistics.

span.label: extends → the NHANES 1999-2000 PFC serum concentrations reported by the same group
span.note: the same survey, the same laboratory, four years later, and the comparison is the paper's point
span.quote: We analyzed the NHANES 1999–2000 and 2003–2004 samples by using two different methods; however, these approaches provided equivalent results [Table 1; Figures S1 and S2 in the Supplemental Material (online at http://www.ehponline.org/docs/2007/10598/suppl.pdf)], indicating that the differences cannot be attributed to changes in the analytical methodology.

span.label: confirms → reported reductions in PFOS and PFOA in Red Cross blood donors and in Arctic ringed seals
span.note: independent populations and an independent species moving the same way over the same interval
span.quote: The decrease in serum concentrations of PFOS and PFOA during this time interval agreed with the reported reductions in PFOS and PFOA concentrations for a group of Red Cross blood donors in the United States and in PFOS (temporal trends for PFOA were not examined) in Arctic ringed seals in the same time.

span.label: serum cotinine —part-of→ Biomonitoring
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.85 — the smoking covariate is itself a biomonitoring measurement, so the model's adjustment shares the exposure measurement's assumptions
span.quote: Participants were categorized as smokers if their serum cotinine concentrations were > 10 μg/L.

span.label: lipophilic POPs —contrasted-with→ half-life
span.note: differs in: how concentration relates to age - lipophilic POPs accumulate with age and these PFCs do not · strength of the relation: 0.95
span.quote: For PFOS, PFOA, and PFNA, however—unlike lipophilic POPs whose serum concentrations increase with age —concentrations were quite similar among the four age groups (Tables 2–5), a finding that agrees with previous data.

span.label: PFBuS —operationalised-as→ limits of detection
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.85 — for the two rarest analytes the LOD is the whole result - no percentile could be computed at all
span.quote: The lower frequency of detection of PFBuS than PFOS, PFOA, and PFHxS suggests that human exposures to PFBuS are indeed lower, and/or that pharmacokinetic factors, which might include increased urinary elimination, are different.

span.label: three PFCs declined and one doubled between the two survey waves
span.quote: The apparent reductions in concentrations of PFOS, PFOA, and PFHxS most likely are related to discontinuation in 2002 of industrial production by electrochemical fluorination of PFOS and related perfluorooctanesulfonyl fluoride compounds.

span.label: unlike lipophilic persistent organic pollutants, these PFCs do not accumulate with age
span.quote: For PFOS, PFOA, and PFNA, however—unlike lipophilic POPs whose serum concentrations increase with age —concentrations were quite similar among the four age groups (Tables 2–5), a finding that agrees with previous data.

span.label: the replacement compound PFBuS was detected in under 0.5% of samples
span.quote: The lower frequency of detection of PFBuS than PFOS, PFOA, and PFHxS suggests that human exposures to PFBuS are indeed lower, and/or that pharmacokinetic factors, which might include increased urinary elimination, are different.

span.label: the two analytical methods agreed on 124 split samples, so the trend is not a method artefact
span.quote: To estimate whether method differences could account for the differences in concentrations, we analyzed QC samples from low and high concentration pools and 124 split samples using both methods. The two methods showed good agreement from the results of the split sample analysis [presented for PFOA in Figures S1 and S2 in Supplemental Material (online at http://www.ehponline.org/docs/2007/10598/suppl.pdf)]. Results were similar for all other analytes (data not shown).

span.label: limits of detection
span.quote: The limits of detection (LODs) ranged from 0.1 to 1.0 μg/L; the accuracy ranged from 84 to 135% at three concentrations; and the precision ranged from around 10 to 26% at two different levels (Table 1).

span.label: smokers
span.quote: Participants were categorized as smokers if their serum cotinine concentrations were > 10 μg/L.

span.label: Race/ethnicity
span.quote: Race/ethnicity was defined on the basis of self-reported data as non-Hispanic black, non-Hispanic white, and Mexican American. Persons not defined by these groups were included only in the total population estimate.

span.label: PFOS, PFOA, PFHxS and PFNA detected in over 98% of 2,094 samples — None
span.quote: Four analytes were detected in > 98% of the samples (PFOS, 99.9%; PFOA, 99.7%; PFHxS, 98.3%; PFNA, 98.8%).

span.label: limits of detection 0.1 to 1.0 ug/L; accuracy 84 to 135%; precision about 10 to 26% — None
span.quote: The limits of detection (LODs) ranged from 0.1 to 1.0 μg/L; the accuracy ranged from 84 to 135% at three concentrations; and the precision ranged from around 10 to 26% at two different levels (Table 1).
